decks.title: Goodwill: Nature and Valuation — Part 1: Meaning, Factors and the Average Profit Methods
goals: Explain goodwill as an intangible asset, its features, and the rule of Accounting Standard 26
Analyse how the factors affecting goodwill raise or lower its value, and say when a firm must value it
Value goodwill by the simple and weighted average profit methods after normalising past profits

slides.heading: Goodwill: Nature and Valuation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **goodwill** is, what makes it rise or fall, when a partnership values it, and the **average profit** methods.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning and nature of goodwill, the factors affecting it, when a firm values it, and the simple and weighted average profit methods
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second chapter of Indian School Certificate Accounts. Imagine two shops on one street with the same capital, yet one earns far more. Customers prefer it, trust it and return to it. That extra earning power has a value, and accountants call it goodwill. In this part we learn what goodwill is, what affects it, when partners must value it, and two methods based on average profit.

slides.heading: What is goodwill?
bullets: **Goodwill** is the value of a business's reputation and connections that lets it earn **more than a normal profit**.
A buyer pays for goodwill because he expects that extra profit to continue.

visual.alt: Table comparing two imagined cycle-repair shops with the same capital of 4,00,000 rupees: both would earn a normal profit of 60,000, but Shop A actually earns 92,000 and Shop B 60,000, so only Shop A earns 32,000 above normal
visual.caption: The extra earning power of Shop A is what a buyer pays for as goodwill.

slides.narration: Here are two imagined cycle repair shops with the same capital. An ordinary shop would earn rupees sixty thousand a year on that capital. Shop B earns just that. Shop A, with loyal customers and a trusted mechanic, earns rupees ninety two thousand. The extra rupees thirty two thousand a year comes from its reputation. Anyone buying Shop A would pay something for that extra earning power. That something is goodwill.

slides.heading: Features of goodwill

rows: Valuable, but cannot be seen or touched
Has a real value that a buyer will pay
Realised only when the whole business is sold
Its value is the earning power expected ahead
Can rise or fall quickly with conditions

visual.alt: Table of six features of goodwill: intangible, not fictitious, inseparable from the business, based on expected future profit, changeable, and hard to value exactly

slides.narration: Goodwill has six features worth remembering. It is intangible: valuable but invisible. It is not fictitious, because a buyer pays real money for it. It cannot be sold apart from the business. Its value rests on profits expected in future, so it changes as conditions change. And because the future is uncertain, different methods give different values.

slides.heading: Quick check: what kind of asset?
slides.narration: Ask yourself two questions. Does goodwill have a physical form? And would a buyer pay real money for it?

slides.heading: Purchased and self-generated goodwill
columns:
**Purchased goodwill**

- Paid for when a business is bought for more than its net assets.
- Recorded in the books as an intangible asset.

**Self-generated goodwill**

- Built up by the firm itself over the years.
- Never recorded: no price was paid, so its cost cannot be measured reliably.

rows: A business is bought for more than its net assets
A firm builds its own reputation over time
Yes, in money or money's worth

visual.alt: Table contrasting purchased goodwill, which arises when a business is bought for more than its net assets, involves a price and is recorded, with self-generated goodwill, which is built by the firm itself, involves no price and is never recorded under Accounting Standard 26

slides.narration: Goodwill comes in two kinds. Purchased goodwill arises when one business buys another and pays more than its net assets are worth; that extra payment is recorded. Self generated goodwill is the reputation a firm builds for itself. Accounting Standard twenty six does not allow it to be recorded, however valuable the partners believe it to be, because no price has been paid.

slides.heading: Factors affecting goodwill

rows: it sits where customers pass and stop
costs are controlled and service is reliable
it holds patents, licences, trademarks or long contracts
it is old, known and trusted
skilled partners and staff stay with the firm

visual.alt: Table of factors affecting goodwill: nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages such as patents and licences, age and reputation, and key people

slides.narration: What makes goodwill high or low? Anything that changes the profits a business can expect. Steady demand, a busy location, efficient management, weak competition and special advantages such as patents, licences or long contracts all raise it. So do an old, trusted name and skilled people who stay. Lose any of these, and goodwill falls.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the factors
slides.body_md: **Phulkari Looms**, an imagined embroidery firm in Patiala, hears three pieces of news in one month. How does each affect its goodwill?

rows: A government emporium chain places a standing order for five years
The master embroiderer, known to every buyer, plans to leave
A cheaper machine-embroidery unit opens in the same bazaar

visual.alt: Table for worked example one: a five-year standing order raises goodwill through special advantages; the planned exit of the master embroiderer lowers it through key people; a cheaper rival in the same bazaar lowers it through the market situation

slides.narration: Take each piece of news and ask what it does to future profits. A five year standing order from an emporium chain assures sales, a special advantage, so goodwill rises. The master embroiderer whom every buyer knows plans to leave, so the key people factor pulls goodwill down. A cheaper rival opening in the same bazaar increases competition, and goodwill falls again.

slides.heading: Quick check: what lowers goodwill?
slides.body_md: Think about the profits the shop can expect.
slides.narration: Which change would send customers, and their money, somewhere else?

slides.heading: When must a firm value goodwill?
bullets: Whenever partners' rights in **future profits** change, someone gains and someone sacrifices.
Recording the value on admission, retirement and death is the subject of **Chapters 3 and 4**.

nodes.label: Amalgamation or sale of the firm

visual.alt: Flow of the occasions on which a partnership values its goodwill: a change in the profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement or death of a partner, and amalgamation or sale of the firm
visual.caption: How the value is then recorded is taught in Chapters 3 and 4.

slides.narration: A partnership must put a value on its goodwill whenever partners' rights in future profits change. That happens when the profit sharing ratio changes, when a partner is admitted, retires or dies, and when the firm is merged or sold. The partner who gains a share must pay the one who sacrifices it. How that payment is recorded comes in chapters three and four.

slides.heading: Methods in your syllabus

nodes.label: Capitalisation of average profit − capital employed

visual.alt: Flow of the five valuation methods in the ISC syllabus: average profit, weighted average profit, super profit, capitalisation of average profit less capital employed, and capitalisation of super profit
visual.caption: Part 1 covers the first two; Part 2 the rest.

slides.narration: The syllabus lists five methods. Two are based on average profit: the simple average and the weighted average. One uses super profit, the profit above normal. Two capitalise a profit: either the average profit, from which capital employed is then deducted, or the super profit itself. We take the average profit methods now and the rest in part two.

slides.heading: The average profit method
bullets: **Goodwill = average profit × number of years' purchase.**
Years' purchase is a multiplier agreed by the partners, not the number of years averaged.

rows: List the profits (or losses) of the agreed past years
Normalise each year: remove items that will not recur
Average profit = total of normal profits ÷ number of years
Deduct expected future costs (fair partner salary, new expenses)
Goodwill = average profit × number of years' purchase

visual.alt: Table of the five steps of the average profit method: list past profits, normalise each year, average them, deduct expected future costs, and multiply by the years of purchase

slides.narration: In the average profit method, goodwill equals the average profit multiplied by a number of years of purchase. First list the past profits, then clean each year of unusual items, then average them. Deduct any cost a buyer will bear in future, such as a fair salary for a partner who works unpaid. Finally multiply by the years of purchase that the partners agree.

slides.heading: Normalising past profits

headers: Item found in a past year
rows: Non-recurring gain (profit on sale of a fixed asset, old insurance claim)
Add back; deduct depreciation each year after
Deduct from (add to) that year; reverse next year
Partner works without salary; new expense ahead
Deduct the fair cost from average profit

visual.alt: Table of normalising adjustments: add back abnormal losses, deduct non-recurring gains and income from non-trade investments, add back capital expenditure charged to revenue less depreciation, correct stock errors in two years, and deduct fair partner salary and expected new expenses

slides.narration: Goodwill is a price for future profits, so past profits must be made normal. Add back abnormal losses such as an uninsured theft. Take out one time gains and income from investments not used in the business. If a machine was wrongly charged as an expense, add it back and charge depreciation instead. Correct stock errors, and charge any fair cost the business will bear in future.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Phulkari Looms, average profit
slides.body_md: Profits: 2022-23 ₹1,86,000; 2023-24 ₹1,68,000; 2024-25 ₹2,64,000; 2025-26 ₹2,58,000. The 2023-24 profit is after an uninsured theft of yarn of ₹36,000; 2024-25 includes ₹30,000 profit on selling an old dyeing vat; 2025-26 includes ₹18,000 dividend on non-trade investments. Goodwill at **3 years' purchase** of average profit.

rows: − 30,000 (gain on sale of dyeing vat deducted)

visual.alt: Table of worked example two: reported profits 1,86,000, 1,68,000, 2,64,000, 2,58,000 rupees; the abnormal loss of 36,000 is added back, the gain of 30,000 and the dividend of 18,000 are deducted, giving normal profits 1,86,000, 2,04,000, 2,34,000, 2,40,000 totalling 8,64,000
visual.caption: Average ₹2,16,000 × 3 years' purchase = goodwill ₹6,48,000.

slides.narration: First make each year normal. Add back the theft of rupees thirty six thousand, which will not recur. Remove the gain of rupees thirty thousand on the old vat, and the dividend of rupees eighteen thousand, which comes from investments outside the business. The four normal profits total rupees eight lakh sixty four thousand, an average of rupees two lakh sixteen thousand. Three years of purchase gives goodwill of rupees six lakh forty eight thousand.

slides.heading: Stock errors touch two years
bullets: Closing stock of one year is the **opening stock** of the next.
Overvalued closing stock: deduct from that year, **add** to the next. Undervalued: the reverse.

visual.alt: Table of a stock error: closing stock of year one overvalued by 12,000 rupees, so year one's profit of 1,50,000 falls to 1,38,000 and year two's profit of 1,40,000 rises to 1,52,000; the two-year total is unchanged
visual.caption: The two-year total does not change; only its split between the years does.

slides.narration: A wrong stock figure affects two years. Suppose the closing stock of year one was overvalued by rupees twelve thousand. Year one's profit was overstated, so we deduct that amount. But the same stock opened year two, raising its cost of goods sold, so year two's profit was understated and we add the amount back. Over the two years the total profit does not change.

slides.heading: Quick check: average profit goodwill
slides.narration: Add the profits, divide by the number of years, and then multiply by the years of purchase.

slides.heading: The weighted average profit method
bullets: Used when profits show a clear **trend**; recent years get the largest weights.
**Weighted average = Σ (profit × weight) ÷ Σ weights.**

visual.alt: Flow of the weighted average method: multiply each normal profit by its weight, add the products, divide by the sum of the weights, and multiply by the years of purchase
visual.caption: Later years get larger weights.

slides.narration: When profits rise or fall steadily, the latest years are the best guide to the future. So we give each year a weight, usually one for the oldest and the largest number for the latest. Multiply each normal profit by its weight, add the products, and divide by the total of the weights. Then multiply by the years of purchase, as before.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Phulkari Looms, weighted average
slides.body_md: Same normal profits, now with weights 1, 2, 3 and 4 for 2022-23 to 2025-26. Goodwill at **3 years' purchase** of the weighted average profit.

visual.alt: Table of worked example three: normal profits 1,86,000, 2,04,000, 2,34,000, 2,40,000 rupees with weights one to four give products totalling 22,56,000; divided by 10 the weighted average is 2,25,600
visual.caption: Weighted average ₹2,25,600 × 3 = goodwill ₹6,76,800.

slides.narration: Multiply each normal profit by its weight. The products add up to rupees twenty two lakh fifty six thousand. The weights add up to ten, so the weighted average profit is rupees two lakh twenty five thousand six hundred. At three years of purchase, goodwill is rupees six lakh seventy six thousand eight hundred, higher than the rupees six lakh forty eight thousand we found with the simple average, because the profits have been rising.

slides.heading: Simple and weighted average compared

visual.alt: Bar chart of Phulkari Looms' normal profits of 186, 204, 234, 240 thousand rupees over four years, with a dashed line at the simple average of 216 thousand and a solid line at the weighted average of 225.6 thousand
visual.caption: Profits trend upward, so the weighted average sits above the simple average.

slides.narration: The bars show the four normal profits of Phulkari Looms. The dashed line is the simple average; the solid line is the weighted average. Because the later, larger profits carry more weight, the weighted line sits higher. If profits had been falling, the weighted average would sit below the simple one.

slides.heading: Quick check: when to weight
slides.body_md: What would make recent years matter more?
slides.narration: Think about when the simple and weighted averages would give nearly the same answer, and when they would not.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Value of earning power above normal; intangible, not fictitious
Anything that changes expected future profits
Any change in partners' rights to future profits
Abnormal losses back, one-time gains out, stock errors in two years, future costs charged
Σ (profit × weight) ÷ Σ weights; × years' purchase

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the meaning of goodwill, the rule of Accounting Standard 26, factors, occasions for valuation, normalising past profits, and the simple and weighted average profit formulas

slides.narration: To sum up. Goodwill is the value of earning power above normal. It is intangible but not fictitious, and only purchased goodwill is recorded. Factors that change expected profits change goodwill, and partners value it whenever their rights in future profits change. Normalise past profits, then multiply the simple or weighted average by the years of purchase.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show a **normal profit table**: year, reported profit, adjustment, normal profit.
A trading **loss** stays in the average: deduct it and still divide by all the years.
Stock errors: correct **two** years, in opposite directions.
Deduct a fair partner salary or a new expense from the **average**, not from one year.
Write the years' purchase in your final line.
slides.narration: Examiners give marks for each step, so set out a normal profit table before you average. Keep an ordinary trading loss in the average and divide by every year. Correct a stock error in both years it touches. Take a fair salary for an unpaid partner from the average profit. And always show the years of purchase in the final line of your answer.

decks.title: Goodwill: Nature and Valuation — Part 2: Capital Employed, Super Profit and Capitalisation
goals: Compute capital employed from a balance sheet, leaving out goodwill, non-trade investments and fictitious assets
Value goodwill as a number of years' purchase of super profit
Value goodwill by capitalising average profit and by capitalising super profit, and explain why the two agree

slides.heading: Capital employed, super profit and capitalisation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **normal profit**, **capital employed**, the **super profit** method and the two **capitalisation** methods.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: normal profit, capital employed, the super profit method, the two capitalisation methods, and a comparison of all methods
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we valued goodwill from average profit alone. But a buyer also asks what his capital could earn elsewhere. In this part we measure the capital employed in a business, work out the normal profit it should earn, and value goodwill from the profit above that, either by a number of years of purchase or by capitalisation.

slides.heading: Normal rate of return and normal profit

rows: Rate that similar firms in the same trade usually earn on capital
Net assets used in the business
Profit an ordinary firm would earn on the same capital

visual.alt: Table of four terms: the normal rate of return earned by similar firms, capital employed as net assets used in the business, normal profit as capital employed times the normal rate, and super profit as average profit minus normal profit

slides.narration: The normal rate of return is what similar firms in the same trade usually earn on their capital. Multiply the capital employed by this rate to get normal profit: what an ordinary business of the same size would earn. Anything a firm earns above that is super profit, and super profit is what a buyer really pays for when he pays for goodwill.

slides.heading: Capital employed (net assets)
bullets: **Capital employed = assets used in the business − outside liabilities.**

rows: It is the very thing being valued
Not used in the business (their income is also removed from profit)
Fictitious assets (debit balance of Profit and Loss, deferred revenue expenditure)
Creditors, bills payable, loans, outstanding expenses

visual.alt: Table of what to leave out when computing capital employed: existing goodwill, non-trade investments and fictitious assets are excluded from assets, and outside liabilities such as creditors, bills payable, loans and outstanding expenses are deducted

slides.narration: Capital employed means the net assets used in the business. Start with the assets, but leave out three things: goodwill already in the books, because that is what we are valuing; non trade investments, which are not used in the business; and fictitious assets, which have no realisable value. Then deduct outside liabilities such as creditors, loans and outstanding expenses.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Sahyadri Cold Chain
slides.body_md: **Sahyadri Cold Chain**, an imagined cold-storage firm in Satara owned by Kedar and Rutuja. Find its capital employed for valuing goodwill.

visual.alt: Horizontal balance sheet of Sahyadri Cold Chain totalling 11,20,000 rupees: capitals of Kedar and Rutuja, general reserve, creditors, bank loan and outstanding wages on the liabilities side; goodwill, plant, building, non-trade investments, stock, debtors, cash and a debit balance of profit and loss on the assets side
visual.caption: Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 (horizontal format)

slides.narration: Here is the balance sheet in the horizontal format used in Indian School Certificate answers, liabilities on the left and assets on the right, each side totalling rupees eleven lakh twenty thousand. Before reading on, find the three assets that must be left out: the goodwill already recorded, the non trade investments, and the debit balance of the profit and loss account.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 (contd): capital employed two ways
columns:
**Assets side**

Assets used: plant, building, stock, debtors, cash = ₹9,60,000

Less outside liabilities ₹3,60,000

**Capital side**

Capitals and reserve = ₹7,60,000

Less goodwill, investments and loss ₹1,60,000

rows: Capitals and reserve 7,60,000 − goodwill, investments and loss 1,60,000

visual.alt: Table of capital employed worked two ways: assets used of 9,60,000 less outside liabilities of 3,60,000, and capitals and reserve of 7,60,000 less excluded items of 1,60,000; both give 6,00,000 rupees
visual.caption: Both routes must give the same answer.

slides.narration: From the assets side, the assets actually used total rupees nine lakh sixty thousand. Deduct outside liabilities of rupees three lakh sixty thousand and capital employed is rupees six lakh. From the capital side, the partners' capitals and reserve total rupees seven lakh sixty thousand; take away the three excluded items and you reach the same rupees six lakh. Use the second route as your check.

slides.heading: Quick check: what counts as capital employed?
slides.body_md: Used in the business, or not?
slides.narration: Only assets that help the business earn its own profit belong in capital employed.

slides.heading: The super profit method
bullets: **Super profit = average profit − normal profit.**
**Goodwill = super profit × number of years' purchase.**

visual.alt: Flow of the super profit method: average profit minus normal profit gives super profit, which is multiplied by the years of purchase to give goodwill
visual.caption: No super profit means no goodwill.

slides.narration: The super profit method values only the profit above normal. Find the average profit, normalised as before. Subtract the normal profit on the capital employed. What remains is super profit. Multiply it by the number of years for which the buyer expects the extra profit to last. If there is no super profit, there is no goodwill.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: super profit at Sahyadri Cold Chain
slides.body_md: Profits: 2023-24 ₹1,10,000; 2024-25 ₹1,22,000; 2025-26 ₹1,34,000, each including ₹8,000 income from the non-trade investments. Normal rate of return 12%. Goodwill at **3 years' purchase of super profit**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example two: normal profits 1,02,000, 1,14,000, 1,26,000 rupees average 1,14,000; normal profit 72,000; super profit 42,000; goodwill 1,26,000 rupees

slides.narration: The investments were left out of capital employed, so their income of rupees eight thousand a year comes out of profit too. The normal profits average rupees one lakh fourteen thousand. Twelve per cent on capital employed of rupees six lakh is a normal profit of rupees seventy two thousand. The super profit is rupees forty two thousand, and three years of purchase gives goodwill of rupees one lakh twenty six thousand.

slides.heading: Where super profit comes from

visual.caption: Each bar is drawn to its own scale; the shaded part is what goodwill pays for.

slides.narration: The upper bar splits the average profit of rupees one lakh fourteen thousand into the normal profit any firm would earn and the super profit that only this firm earns. The lower bar shows the same idea for capital: the capitalised value of rupees nine lakh fifty thousand is capital employed plus goodwill. The shaded parts are what goodwill pays for.

slides.heading: Quick check: super profit goodwill
slides.body_md: Normal profit, super profit, then years' purchase.
slides.narration: Follow the same three steps as the cold chain example, in the same order.

slides.heading: Capitalisation of average profit
bullets: **Capitalised value = average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate.**
**Goodwill = capitalised value − capital employed.**

visual.alt: Flow of capitalisation of average profit: average profit times one hundred divided by the normal rate gives the capitalised value, from which capital employed is deducted to give goodwill
visual.caption: Capitalised value: the capital a normal firm would need to earn this profit.

slides.narration: Capitalisation asks a different question: how much capital would an ordinary firm need to earn this firm's average profit at the normal rate? That figure is the capitalised value. The firm actually uses less capital than that. The difference between the capitalised value and the capital employed is goodwill.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: capitalising average profit
slides.body_md: Sahyadri Cold Chain: average profit ₹1,14,000, normal rate 12%, capital employed ₹6,00,000.

visual.alt: Table of worked example three: capitalised value of 9,50,000 rupees less capital employed of 6,00,000 gives goodwill of 3,50,000

slides.narration: An ordinary cold store earning twelve per cent would need rupees nine lakh fifty thousand of capital to make rupees one lakh fourteen thousand a year. Sahyadri does it with only rupees six lakh. The difference, rupees three lakh fifty thousand, is its goodwill by capitalising the average profit.

slides.heading: Capitalisation of super profit
bullets: **Goodwill = super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate.**

visual.alt: Table showing that capitalising super profit equals average profit times one hundred over the rate minus capital employed, which is the capitalisation of average profit

slides.narration: The second capitalisation method capitalises the super profit directly: multiply it by one hundred and divide by the normal rate. The table shows why this must agree with the first method. Replace super profit by average profit minus normal profit, simplify, and you are back to the capitalised value of average profit minus capital employed.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: capitalising super profit
slides.body_md: Sahyadri Cold Chain: super profit ₹42,000, normal rate 12%.

visual.alt: Table of worked example four: capitalising the super profit of 42,000 at 12 per cent gives 3,50,000 rupees, the same as capitalising the average profit
visual.caption: Same figures, same rate, same goodwill.

slides.narration: Capitalise the super profit of rupees forty two thousand at twelve per cent: multiply by one hundred and divide by twelve. The answer is rupees three lakh fifty thousand, exactly what the first method gave. When the two methods disagree in your working, check your normal profit or your capital employed.

slides.heading: Quick check: do the capitalisation methods agree?
slides.narration: Recall the algebra on the previous slides before you answer.

slides.heading: No super profit, no goodwill

visual.alt: Table of a firm with capital employed of 5,00,000 rupees, normal profit of 60,000 and average profit of only 54,000: there is no super profit, so goodwill is nil

slides.narration: A firm can have plenty of profit and still no goodwill. This imagined firm employs rupees five lakh, so at twelve per cent it should earn rupees sixty thousand. It earns only rupees fifty four thousand. There is no profit above normal, so the super profit and capitalisation methods both give no goodwill. Never multiply a shortfall by the years of purchase.

slides.heading: One firm, every method

rows: Excess earning power, without limit of time
The same, by the other formula

visual.alt: Comparison table for Sahyadri Cold Chain: average profit method 3,42,000 rupees, super profit method 1,26,000, and both capitalisation methods 3,50,000
visual.caption: Methods differ because they pay for different things; the partners agree the method in advance.

slides.narration: Here is Sahyadri Cold Chain valued four ways. The average profit method pays for all profit for three years, rupees three lakh forty two thousand. The super profit method pays only for the excess for three years, rupees one lakh twenty six thousand. The capitalisation methods treat the excess as lasting indefinitely, rupees three lakh fifty thousand. That is why partners must agree the method in advance.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and nature of goodwill
sections.body_md:
**Goodwill** is the value of the reputation, customer connections and other advantages that enable a business to earn **more than a normal profit**. A buyer pays for it because he expects that extra profit to continue.

**Features:**
- **Intangible**: valuable, but without physical existence.
- **Not fictitious**: it has a real value that can be realised on a sale of the business.
- **Inseparable**: it cannot be sold apart from the business.
- **Based on expected future profits**, so it can change quickly.
- **Subjective**: different methods give different values; partners agree the method.

key_terms.definition_md: The value of a business's ability to earn profit above the normal profit of similar businesses.
An asset with value but no physical form, such as goodwill, patents and trademarks.
A loss or expense not yet written off, with no realisable value (for example a debit balance of Profit and Loss).

sections.heading: 2. Purchased and self-generated goodwill; Accounting Standard 26
sections.body_md:
**Purchased goodwill** arises when a business is bought for more than the fair value of its net assets; the excess paid is goodwill.

**Self-generated (internally generated) goodwill** is built by the firm itself.

**Accounting Standard 26 (Intangible Assets):** only goodwill acquired for a consideration in money or money's worth is recorded. Self-generated goodwill is **not** recorded, because its cost cannot be measured reliably.

In a partnership, goodwill is usually **valued** (not recorded) on reconstitution; how the value is adjusted among partners is covered in Chapters 3 and 4.

sections.heading: 3. Factors affecting goodwill
sections.body_md:
Goodwill rises or falls with the profits a business can expect. The main factors:
- **Nature of business:** steady demand, stable products.
- **Location:** a site customers reach easily.
- **Efficiency of management:** low costs, reliable service.
- **Market situation:** little or no competition.
- **Special advantages:** patents, trademarks, licences, import quotas, long-term contracts, cheap power or raw material.
- **Age and reputation:** an old, trusted name.
- **Key people:** skilled owners or staff who stay.

**Rule of thumb:** ask whether a change will raise or lower **future profits**.

sections.heading: 6. Weighted average profit method
sections.body_md:
Used when profits show a **clear trend**. Recent years receive larger weights (usually 1, 2, 3 … from the oldest).

**Weighted average profit = Σ (normal profit × weight) ÷ Σ weights**

**Goodwill = weighted average profit × number of years' purchase.**

Rising profits: weighted average > simple average. Falling profits: weighted average < simple average. Steady profits: nearly equal.

key_terms.definition_md: A number showing the relative importance given to a year's profit.
The sum of each profit multiplied by its weight, divided by the sum of the weights.

sections.heading: 7. Capital employed and the super profit method
sections.body_md:
**Capital employed (net assets)** = total assets − goodwill already in the books − non-trade investments − fictitious assets − outside liabilities.

Check from the capital side: partners' capitals + reserves + credit balance of Profit and Loss − goodwill − non-trade investments − fictitious assets.

**Normal profit** = capital employed × normal rate of return ÷ 100.

**Super profit** = average profit − normal profit.

**Goodwill = super profit × number of years' purchase.** If super profit is nil or negative, there is **no goodwill**.

When non-trade investments are left out of capital employed, their income is removed from profit as well.

sections.heading: 8. Capitalisation methods and comparison
sections.body_md:
**Capitalisation of average profit:**
- capitalised value = average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate of return;
- goodwill = capitalised value − capital employed.

**Capitalisation of super profit:** goodwill = super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate of return.

With the same figures and rate the two always agree: super profit × 100 ÷ rate = average profit × 100 ÷ rate − capital employed.

**Comparing methods:** the average profit method pays for all profit for a few years; the super profit method pays for the excess for a few years; the capitalisation methods value the excess earning power without a time limit. Partners agree the method in the deed or at the time of valuation.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts, Section A)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, term or assertion-reason choice.
- 2 marks: a feature or occasion with its reason, or a one-step valuation (normal profit and goodwill).
- 3 marks: a valuation with one or two normalising adjustments, or capital employed from a short balance sheet.
- 5 marks: capital employed from a horizontal balance sheet plus super profit or capitalisation goodwill; or five years' profits with several adjustments.

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying by the number of years averaged instead of the years' purchase.
- Leaving an abnormal loss in, or a one-time gain in, before averaging.
- Correcting a stock error in only one year.
- Including existing goodwill, non-trade investments or a debit balance of Profit and Loss in capital employed.
- Removing non-trade investments from capital employed but leaving their income in profit.
- Calculating normal profit on average profit instead of on capital employed.
- Showing a negative goodwill instead of stating that there is no goodwill.
- Forgetting to deduct capital employed when capitalising average profit.

All firms and figures in SOYL practice are imagined; the board paper gives its own.

questions.stem_md: An imagined tea stall beside the bus depot in Dharwad has regulars who return every morning, so it earns more than the stall across the road. For accounts, the value of this pull on customers (its goodwill) is classed as

options.text_md: a fictitious asset
an intangible asset
a current asset
an outside liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an intangible asset. Goodwill has a real value that a buyer pays for, but no physical form. A fictitious asset, such as a debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account, has no realisable value at all.

questions.stem_md: The partners of an imagined pottery studio in Khurja estimate that the reputation they have built over twelve years is worth ₹2,00,000, and want to show it on the assets side of their balance sheet. Under Accounting Standard 26 (Intangible Assets) they

options.text_md: may do so, provided every partner signs the entry
may do so, but only at half of the estimated value
must do so, because goodwill is a real asset
cannot do so, because goodwill is recorded only when it has been acquired for a consideration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cannot do so, because goodwill is recorded only when it has been acquired for a consideration. Goodwill built up inside the business cannot be measured reliably, so it is never brought into the books. Only purchased goodwill, paid for in money or money's worth, is recorded.

questions.stem_md: Which event is most likely to **reduce** the goodwill of an imagined optician's shop in Shillong?

options.text_md: The partner whose eye tests draw most customers retires and opens a shop across the road
The shop wins the sole franchise in the city for a popular lens brand
A new district hospital opens next door
The shop completes thirty years of trading under the same name

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The partner whose eye tests draw most customers retires and opens a shop across the road. When the person customers trust leaves, and takes them to a rival, the profits the shop can expect fall. The other three events would raise its goodwill.

questions.stem_md: An imagined sports-goods maker in Jalandhar is about to value its goodwill. Which development would **raise** that value?

options.text_md: A larger rival opens a factory in the same industrial area
Its chief bat designer leaves to start his own unit
It is granted a patent on a new grip for cricket-bat handles
Import duty on foreign bats is cut, so they become cheaper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is granted a patent on a new grip for cricket-bat handles. A patent is a special advantage: it protects future sales and profits. More competition, the loss of key talent and cheaper imports all lower expected profits.

questions.stem_md: Partners must agree a value for their firm's goodwill whenever their rights in future profits change. In which situation is a valuation of goodwill **not** needed?

options.text_md: A new partner is admitted
A partner retires from the firm
A partner brings in additional capital and the profit-sharing ratio stays the same
The existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A partner brings in additional capital and the profit-sharing ratio stays the same. Extra capital with an unchanged ratio leaves every partner's share of future profits as it was, so no partner gains or sacrifices goodwill.

questions.stem_md: A buyer agrees to pay more than the value of the net assets for an imagined flower-wholesale business in Madurai. The extra amount is paid for

options.text_md: the chance to earn more than a normal profit in future, thanks to the business's name and connections
the profits the business has already earned in past years
the cash and bank balances taken over
the creditors the buyer agrees to pay

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the chance to earn more than a normal profit in future, thanks to the business's name and connections. Goodwill is valued on expected future profits. Past profits belong to the old owners, and cash or creditors are already part of the net assets.

questions.stem_md: Unlike a delivery van or a stock of goods owned by a firm, goodwill

options.text_md: can be sold separately at any time
loses its whole value at the end of every accounting year
is always shown at whatever value the partners estimate
cannot be sold on its own; it is realised only when the business as a whole is sold

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cannot be sold on its own; it is realised only when the business as a whole is sold. Goodwill is attached to the business itself, so it is realised only on a sale of the business.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Intangible:** goodwill has value but no physical existence.

2. **Inseparable:** it cannot be sold apart from the business; it is realised only when the business is sold.

*(Also accepted: its value depends on expected future profits; it is a valuable, not fictitious, asset; its value can change quickly with conditions; only purchased goodwill is recorded under Accounting Standard 26.)*

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between **purchased goodwill** and **self-generated goodwill** on any two points.
questions.solution_md: Contrast how each arises and whether it may be recorded.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Purchased goodwill | Self-generated goodwill |
|---|---|---|
| How it arises | Paid for when a business is bought for more than its net assets | Built up by the firm over time through its own reputation |

questions.stem_md: Give any **two** occasions on which a partnership firm needs to value its goodwill, with a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Valuation is needed whenever partners' rights in future profits change.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Admission of a partner:** the newcomer will share future profits the old partners' reputation produced, so he must compensate them for their sacrifice.

2. **Retirement or death of a partner:** the outgoing partner (or the legal heir) gives up a share of future profits and must be paid for his share of goodwill by the gaining partners.

*(Also accepted: a change in the profit-sharing ratio; amalgamation of firms; sale of the business.)*

questions.stem_md: An imagined bamboo-craft firm in Agartala faces three changes in 2026: (i) the partner whose designs win most export orders retires and joins a competitor; (ii) the showroom moves from the main market to a narrow back lane to save rent; (iii) the firm signs an exclusive five-year contract to supply a hotel chain. For each change, state its likely effect on the firm's goodwill and name the factor involved.
questions.solution_md: Judge each change by its effect on the profits the firm can expect to earn.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **(i) Goodwill falls** (efficiency and skill of the people running the business): the export orders, and the profits they bring, are likely to follow the designer to the rival.

2. **(ii) Goodwill falls** (location): fewer customers will find a shop in a back lane, so expected sales drop even though rent is saved.

3. **(iii) Goodwill rises** (special advantages): a long exclusive contract assures steady profits for five years.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: "Goodwill is just a figure the partners invent, so it is a fictitious asset." Correct the student, explaining why goodwill is an **intangible** asset and **not** a fictitious one.
questions.solution_md: Separate "no physical form" from "no realisable value".

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Intangible:** goodwill cannot be seen or touched, yet it is valuable, because it lets the firm earn more than a normal profit.

2. **Not fictitious:** a fictitious asset (for example a debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account) is a loss or expense not yet written off and can never be sold; goodwill can be realised in cash when the business is sold, and a buyer pays real money for it.

3. **Not invented:** goodwill is valued from the firm's profits by agreed methods, and Accounting Standard 26 lets it be recorded only when it has been paid for.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning of intangible, applied to goodwill
Valued from profits / recorded only when purchased

questions.stem_md: Before the average profit of an imagined dairy-equipment dealer is used to value its goodwill, its past profits are "normalised". Explain why, giving two examples of adjustments.
questions.solution_md: Link normalising to maintainable future profit, then give two adjustments.

answer.model_answer_md:
Goodwill is a price paid for **future** profits, so only profits the business can expect to keep earning should be averaged. Items that will not happen again would give a misleading value.

Examples: (1) an abnormal loss, such as an uninsured theft, is **added back**; (2) a non-recurring gain, such as profit on selling a fixed asset, is **deducted**. *(Also accepted: income from non-trade investments deducted; fair remuneration of a working partner deducted; stock errors corrected; expected future expenses charged.)*

questions.stem_md: The average profit of an imagined silver-filigree workshop in Cuttack is ₹1,50,000. One partner works full time in the workshop but draws no salary; a manager doing the same work would cost ₹36,000 a year. Value goodwill at **two years' purchase** of the average profit.
questions.solution_md: A buyer would have to pay someone for that work, so its fair cost is charged before goodwill is valued.

answer.model_answer_md:
Average profit after a fair reward for the partner's work = ₹1,50,000 − ₹36,000 = ₹1,14,000.

Goodwill = ₹1,14,000 × 2 = **₹2,28,000**.

A new partner is to pay for his share of goodwill, valued at **two years' purchase**. Calculate goodwill by (a) the simple average and (b) the weighted average (weights 1 to 4), and (c) say which is fairer to the incoming partner, and why.
questions.solution_md: Weighting pulls the average towards recent years, which matters when there is a trend.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Simple average = 7,80,000 ÷ 4 = ₹1,95,000; goodwill = **₹3,90,000**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined book-binding firm in Dehradun earned ₹2,10,000, ₹2,40,000, ₹2,70,000 in its last three years. Both partners work full time without salary; a fair salary would be ₹30,000 a year each. The machinery has never been insured; from next year an annual premium of ₹6,000 will be paid. Value goodwill at **three years' purchase** of the future maintainable profit.
questions.solution_md: Charge every cost a buyer would actually bear in future before applying the years' purchase.

answer.model_answer_md:
Average profit = 2,10,000 + 2,40,000 + 2,70,000 = 7,20,000; ÷ 3 = ₹2,40,000.

Less: fair salary of two partners ₹60,000; insurance premium ₹6,000. Future maintainable profit = 2,40,000 − 60,000 − 6,000 = ₹1,74,000.

Goodwill = ₹1,74,000 × 3 = **₹5,22,000**.

On checking the books: (i) the 2022-23 profit is after an uninsured theft of carved panels worth ₹40,000; (ii) on 1 April 2023 a polishing machine costing ₹50,000 was bought and wrongly charged to revenue; machinery is depreciated at 10% a year on the straight-line method. questions.solution_md: Abnormal loss back in; capital expenditure back in for the year of purchase, then depreciation out for every year the machine was used.

questions.stem_md: An imagined chilli-trading firm in Guntur reported profits of ₹2,00,000 in 2022-23, ₹2,30,000 in 2023-24, ₹2,10,000 in 2024-25, ₹2,70,000 in 2025-26. The 2023-24 profit includes a gain of ₹30,000 on selling a spare warehouse plot; the 2024-25 profit is after a loss of ₹40,000 when cyclone rain ruined stock in an uninsured godown. (a) Value goodwill at **two years' purchase of the weighted average profit**, using weights 1, 2, 3 and 4. (b) Find goodwill on the simple average for comparison, and explain the difference.
questions.solution_md: Normalise first (gain out, abnormal loss back in), then weight; the trend explains the gap between the two values.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Normal profits and weights:

| Year | Normal profit (₹) | Weight | Product (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-23 | 2,00,000 | 1 | 2,00,000 |
| 2023-24 | 2,00,000 | 2 | 4,00,000 |
| 2024-25 | 2,50,000 | 3 | 7,50,000 |
| 2025-26 | 2,70,000 | 4 | 10,80,000 |
| **Total** |  | **10** | **24,30,000** |

Weighted average profit = 24,30,000 ÷ 10 = ₹2,43,000; goodwill = ₹2,43,000 × 2 = **₹4,86,000**.

**(b)** Simple average = 9,20,000 ÷ 4 = ₹2,30,000; goodwill = **₹4,60,000**. The weighted value is higher because the normal profits rise over the period and the latest, largest profit carries weight 4.

questions.stem_md: An imagined perfume (attar) maker in Kannauj reported profits of ₹1,60,000 for 2023-24, ₹1,80,000 for 2024-25, ₹2,15,000 for 2025-26. While preparing for a partner's retirement, the partners find that the stock on 31 March 2024 was **overvalued** by ₹20,000 and the stock on 31 March 2025 was **undervalued** by ₹10,000. (a) Explain why one stock error affects the profits of two years. (b) Correct the profits and value goodwill at **two years' purchase** of the average profit.
questions.solution_md: Trace each wrong stock figure into both years it touches, then average.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The closing stock of one year is the opening stock of the next. A closing stock that is too high raises that year's profit; as the next year's opening stock it raises cost of goods sold and lowers that year's profit by the same amount (and the reverse for undervaluation). Over the two years the errors cancel.

**(b)**

| Year | Profit as reported (₹) | Adjustment (₹) | Normal profit (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-24 | 1,60,000 | − 20,000 (closing stock overvalued) | 1,40,000 |
| 2024-25 | 1,80,000 | + 20,000 (opening stock overvalued); + 10,000 (closing stock undervalued) | 2,10,000 |
| 2025-26 | 2,15,000 | − 10,000 (opening stock undervalued) | 2,05,000 |
| **Total** | **5,55,000** |  | **5,55,000** |

Average profit = 5,55,000 ÷ 3 = ₹1,85,000; goodwill = ₹1,85,000 × 2 = **₹3,70,000**.

questions.stem_md: The partners of an imagined jaggery-trading firm in Kolhapur plan to admit a new partner and must value goodwill. (a) Distinguish between purchased and self-generated goodwill, and state which of them the firm may record in its books. (b) Their accountant says goodwill must be valued on "future maintainable profit". Explain this idea, with **three** adjustments she will make to the past profits.
questions.solution_md: Part (a): origin and recording rule; part (b): meaning, then any three adjustments.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Purchased goodwill arises when a business is acquired for more than its net assets; a price has actually been paid. Self-generated goodwill is the reputation a firm builds for itself; no price has been paid and its cost cannot be measured. Under Accounting Standard 26 only purchased goodwill may be recorded.

**(b)** A new partner pays for the profits the firm can go on earning, not for what happened by chance in past years. So the past profits are cleaned of items that will not recur and charged with costs that will arise. Adjustments: (1) abnormal losses such as an uninsured theft are added back; (2) non-recurring gains such as profit on sale of a fixed asset are deducted; (3) a fair salary for a partner who works without pay is deducted. *(Also accepted: income from non-trade investments removed; stock errors corrected; known future expenses such as a new insurance premium charged.)*

questions.stem_md: A partner of an imagined handloom house in Imphal claims ₹18,000 as goodwill at three years' purchase of super profit. The firm employs ₹8,00,000, the normal rate of return is 12% and its average profit is ₹90,000. Is the claim correct? Show your working.

A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the capitalised value is average profit × 100 ÷ normal rate, the capital that would earn that profit at the normal rate.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The accountant of an imagined river-ferry service values its goodwill twice from one set of figures at a normal rate of 12%: first by capitalising the super profit, then by capitalising the average profit and deducting the capital employed. If her arithmetic is right, the two answers will be equal.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Super profit × 100 ÷ rate = (average profit − capital employed × rate ÷ 100) × 100 ÷ rate = average profit × 100 ÷ rate − capital employed. The two methods are the same formula rearranged.

questions.stem_md: An imagined tour operator in Gangtok earns an average profit of ₹1,26,000 on capital employed of ₹7,50,000. The normal rate of return for tour operators is 14%. Find its goodwill by **capitalising the average profit** (in ₹).

An imagined silk-weaving firm in Bhagalpur earns ₹21,000 a year more than a normal firm of its size (its super profit). The normal rate of return in weaving is 15%. Find its goodwill by **capitalising the super profit** (in ₹).

An imagined incense-stick (agarbatti) maker in Mysuru earns an average profit of ₹96,000 on capital employed of ₹6,00,000. The normal rate of return is 12%. Value its goodwill by **capitalising the super profit**.
questions.solution_md: Find the super profit first, then capitalise it at the normal rate.

questions.stem_md: The goodwill of an imagined art-plate workshop in Thanjavur, found by capitalising its average profit, is ₹1,60,000. Its capital employed is ₹6,40,000 and the normal rate of return is 12.5%. Work backwards to find its average profit.
questions.solution_md: Reverse the method: rebuild the capitalised value, then apply the normal rate to it.

answer.model_answer_md:
Capitalised value of average profit = goodwill + capital employed = ₹1,60,000 + ₹6,40,000 = ₹8,00,000.

Average profit = ₹8,00,000 × 12.5 ÷ 100 = **₹1,00,000**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined mustard-oil mill in Alwar earned profits of ₹1,85,000, ₹2,05,000, ₹2,25,000 in its last three years. Its assets (there is no goodwill or fictitious asset in the books) total ₹18,00,000 and its outside liabilities ₹4,00,000. The normal rate of return is 12.5%. Value goodwill by **capitalising the average profit**.
questions.solution_md: Capitalise the average profit at the normal rate and subtract the net assets actually used.

questions.stem_md: Two partners of an imagined tea-packaging firm in Siliguri disagree: one wants goodwill by capitalising the average profit, the other by capitalising the super profit. Average profit is ₹1,08,000, capital employed ₹8,00,000 and the normal rate of return 12%. Work out both values and settle the dispute.
questions.solution_md: Compute both; the agreement follows algebraically from normal profit = capital employed × rate.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Capitalising average profit: 1,08,000 × 100 ÷ 12 = ₹9,00,000; less capital employed 8,00,000 = **₹1,00,000**.

2. Capitalising super profit: normal profit = 8,00,000 × 12 ÷ 100 = 96,000; super profit = 12,000; × 100 ÷ 12 = **₹1,00,000**.

3. Both give the same goodwill, so the choice of method does not matter here: the two methods are one formula written two ways when the same figures and rate are used.

questions.stem_md:
Sushanta and Lipika own an imagined steel-fabrication shop in Rourkela. Their Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 was:

| Liabilities | ₹ | Assets | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sushanta's Capital | 6,00,000 | Goodwill | 80,000 |
| Lipika's Capital | 4,50,000 | Land and Building | 6,00,000 |
| General Reserve | 1,00,000 | Plant | 4,50,000 |
| Creditors | 1,10,000 | Non-trade Investments | 70,000 |
| Bank Loan | 2,40,000 | Stock | 1,50,000 |
|  |  | Debtors | 1,20,000 |
|  |  | Cash | 30,000 |
| **Total** | **15,00,000** | **Total** | **15,00,000** |

The shop's profits for 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 were ₹1,47,000, ₹1,57,000, ₹1,67,000, each including a dividend of ₹7,000 on the non-trade investments. The normal rate of return is 12%. (a) Find the capital employed. (b) Value goodwill by capitalising the average profit. (c) Value goodwill by capitalising the super profit.
questions.solution_md: Exclude the investments from both capital employed and profit; the two capitalisation answers must agree.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Capital employed = assets used in the business ₹13,50,000 − outside liabilities ₹3,50,000 = **₹10,00,000** (goodwill 80,000 and non-trade investments 70,000 left out).

**(b)** Average profit after removing the dividends = (1,40,000 + 1,50,000 + 1,60,000) ÷ 3 = ₹1,50,000. Capitalised value = 1,50,000 × 100 ÷ 12 = ₹12,50,000. Goodwill = 12,50,000 − 10,00,000 = **₹2,50,000**.

**(c)** Normal profit = 10,00,000 × 12 ÷ 100 = ₹1,20,000; super profit = 1,50,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹30,000. Goodwill = 30,000 × 100 ÷ 12 = **₹2,50,000**, the same as in (b).

questions.stem_md: An imagined homestay business in Munnar is to be sold. Its profits for the last four years were ₹1,30,000, ₹1,40,000, ₹1,60,000, ₹1,70,000; capital employed is ₹10,00,000 and the normal rate of return 10%. (a) Value goodwill by (i) three years' purchase of average profit, (ii) three years' purchase of super profit and (iii) capitalisation of super profit. (b) The buyer insists on method (ii). Evaluate whether his position is reasonable.
questions.solution_md: Compare what each method pays for: all profit, excess profit for a few years, or excess profit for ever.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Average profit = 6,00,000 ÷ 4 = ₹1,50,000; normal profit = 10,00,000 × 10 ÷ 100 = ₹1,00,000; super profit = ₹50,000.

| Method | Working | Goodwill (₹) |
|---|---|---|
| (i) Average profit | 1,50,000 × 3 | 4,50,000 |
| (ii) Super profit | 50,000 × 3 | 1,50,000 |
| (iii) Capitalisation of super profit | 50,000 × 100 ÷ 10 | 5,00,000 |

**(b)** Reasonable: the buyer must put in ₹10,00,000 of capital, which would earn ₹1,00,000 anywhere at the normal rate, so only the excess of ₹50,000 a year is due to the business's reputation. Method (i) charges him for normal profit too. But three years' purchase assumes the excess lasts only three years; if the homestay's reputation is likely to last, capitalising the super profit (as if it continues indefinitely) is fairer to the seller, so the years' purchase should be negotiated.

questions.stem_md: The seller of an imagined dhaba on a Punjab highway offers the buyer four ways to price its goodwill. Match each valuation formula with what the buyer is really paying for under it.

options.text_md: Average profit × years' purchase
Weighted average profit × years' purchase
Super profit × years' purchase
Super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate

match_right.text_md: The profit above normal, with no time limit
All the profit, with recent years counting more
Only the profit above normal, for a fixed number of years
All the profit, for a fixed number of years

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Average-profit methods pay for the whole profit; super-profit methods pay only for the excess over what the capital would earn anyway; capitalising treats the excess as lasting indefinitely.

questions.stem_md: While calculating the capital employed of an imagined cold-drinks bottler for goodwill, which balance-sheet item is **included** in the assets?

options.text_md: Goodwill bought when the firm took over a rival
Shares of an unrelated company held as non-trade investments
Bottling machinery used in the plant
Debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bottling machinery used in the plant. Capital employed counts only assets used to earn the business's profit. Existing goodwill, non-trade investments and fictitious assets are left out.

questions.stem_md: An imagined footwear wholesaler in Ambur has total assets of ₹9,40,000, including goodwill of ₹60,000 and non-trade investments of ₹80,000. Its outside liabilities are ₹2,00,000. Its capital employed for valuing goodwill is

**Assertion (A):** Goodwill already appearing in a firm's balance sheet is left out when capital employed is calculated for valuing goodwill.

**Reason (R):** Goodwill is an intangible asset.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: other intangibles used in the business, such as patents, are included. Goodwill is left out because it is the very thing being valued.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account on the assets side of an imagined hardware store's balance sheet is left out of its capital employed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** It is a fictitious asset (an accumulated loss), not an asset used in the business, so it is excluded.

questions.stem_md: For valuing a firm's goodwill, capital employed = total assets (excluding goodwill, non-trade investments and fictitious assets) − ___ liabilities.
questions.solution_md: Deduct the outside (external) liabilities: creditors, bills payable, loans and outstanding expenses.

questions.stem_md: An imagined electronics-repair firm in Hosur shows total assets of ₹6,50,000, including goodwill of ₹40,000 and a debit balance of ₹10,000 in the Profit and Loss Account. Its creditors are ₹90,000 and its bank overdraft ₹60,000. Calculate its capital employed (in ₹).

An imagined auto-parts firm in Rajkot gives only the capital side of its balance sheet: partners' capitals ₹5,00,000 and ₹3,00,000, General Reserve ₹70,000 and a credit balance of ₹30,000 in the Profit and Loss Account. The assets include goodwill of ₹40,000 and non-trade investments of ₹60,000. Calculate the capital employed.
questions.solution_md: From the capital side: partners' funds less the assets that do not count.

answer.model_answer_md:
Capitals and reserves = 5,00,000 + 3,00,000 + 70,000 + 30,000 = ₹9,00,000.

Capital employed = 9,00,000 − goodwill 40,000 − non-trade investments 60,000 = **₹8,00,000**.
